body.text: As competition between the United States and China over artificial intelligence, advanced semiconductors, and technological supremacy intensifies, the resignation of Nvidia founder Jensen Huang hit like a bombshell. The controversy extends far beyond a shakeup in the Nvidia boardroom. CollegeDaily, a Chinese-language digital media outlet with commercial roots in China and an audience among overseas Chinese students, described Huang’s downfall as “a tragedy for millions of Chinese Americans.”

Why should an entrepreneur who was born in Taiwan, grew up in the United States become a symbol of the fate of the entire Chinese American ethnic community? More strikingly, Huang had reached the pinnacle of American technological power – he built one of the world’s most important AI chip companies – yet some Chinese-language commentators portrayed him as an outsider who could never be fully accepted by American society.

Such anxieties are not without foundation, as the news coverage showed. As Huang’s extramarital affairs – and allegations that one of the women was involved in Chinese intelligence activities – attracted attention, some American media coverage and social media reactions exposed familiar racial and gender stereotypes. The New York Post ran the headline “HUANG HUANG BANG BANG,” while The Economist used the pun “Two Huangs Don’t Make a Right,” turning an Asian surname into a joke about a sex scandal. The Asian American Journalists Association (AAJA) criticized such coverage.

On social media, the mockery was more explicit. A photograph of an Asian woman circulated with the caption “How your Chinese gf looks at you before asking for state secrets,” suggesting that Chinese women might exploit intimate relationships to obtain classified information. Other posts assembled photographs of Chinese partners of other prominent American technology executives, as though their ethnicity alone warranted suspicion. Chinese media responded with article titles like, “Why Has the Siege of Nvidia Turned into a Racial Witch Hunt?”

In parts of Chinese-language commentary, questions of personal misconduct, corporate governance, and national security were sidelined in favor of another explanation: Huang had been taken down by the U.S. establishment. Hu Xijin, the former editor-in-chief of the Global Times and an influential voice in Chinese nationalist commentary, speculated that U.S. intelligence agencies had supplied damaging material to The New York Times, using media exposure and stock market pressure to force Nvidia’s board into action. “This is almost a ‘coup’ aimed at driving a Chinese founder out of America’s most important high-tech company,” Hu said in a post on X. “This incident will have a profound impact on the situation of Chinese people in the United States.”

In this interpretation, the affair was merely the opening through which a political operation could proceed. The real issue was supposedly the American establishment’s unwillingness to tolerate a Chinese American at the helm of such a strategically important company. In this viewing, Huang is not simply an American executive facing questions about his conduct and corporate responsibilities; he is an ethnic casualty of the China-U.S. technology rivalry. In a follow-up post, Hu warned: “If even Jensen Huang can be driven out so casually, then removing a Chinese person from some other, less prominent position would require even less hesitation.”

Rao Yi, a prominent Chinese scientist at Peking University, published an article on his WeChat public account titled “The Jensen Huang Affair Proves That Every Overseas Chinese Experiences Racial Discrimination.” This article highlighted not only perceived discrimination against Huang, but the assumptions being made about Alice Huang, the Chinese business executive Jensen Huang is believed to have had a romantic relationship with.

Similar concerns surfaced in Chinese-language WeChat groups I observed in Canada. Some participants asked why other American executives caught in sex scandals had not faced comparable consequences. Others even worried that Huang’s children, who already worked at Nvidia, might also be pushed out of the company.

These reactions did not necessarily arise from the same political convictions, but they converged on a common question: How successful must a person of Chinese descent become before feeling secure against exclusion on the basis of ethnicity?

What makes Huang’s case particularly revealing is how high he rose before his fall. He possessed enormous wealth, led a globally dominant technology company, and had direct access to American political leaders – including U.S. President Donald Trump. Yet in some Chinese-language narratives, even these advantages could not protect his position.

TechFlow, an influential Chinese-language technology and investment publication, summarized his predicament: “He has the chips, but not the microphone.” It contrasted Huang with Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, and Rupert Murdoch, business magnates who own major media properties or communications platforms. For all his influence, TechFlow argued, Huang was unable to shape the narrative.

As usual, online opinion had a more cutting phrase: “The law doesn’t reach Epstein’s island, but respect doesn’t extend to bananas.” The phrase juxtaposed the perceived impunity of U.S. elites implicated in the child sex abuse case linked to Jeffrey Epstein with the vulnerability of assimilated Chinese Americans, who are derogatorily described as “bananas.” The implication is that Huang’s wealth, technological achievements, and political influence could not offset the vulnerability of being a Chinese American.

The flip side of this narrative is the assumption that more powerful forces were working against Huang. Jinse Finance, an established Chinese-language blockchain and cryptocurrency news outlet, mapped ten forces allegedly involved in Huang’s downfall, including mainstream media outlets, Congress, Wall Street, intelligence agencies, technology companies, and Nvidia insiders. The article alleged that the main actor pulling the strings was Anthropic, acting out of corporate rivalry to co-opt anti-Chinese sentiment in Washington and beyond. In this framing, and other articles like it, Huang’s personal conduct receded from view as his fate became part of a larger, more opaque struggle for power.

When Huang becomes a symbol of an entire ethnic community, criticism of him can also be interpreted as a betrayal of that community. Indian American writer Anand Giridharadas published a satirical piece in The New York Times referencing Huang’s signature leather jacket, titled, “Jensen Huang Betrayed the Leather Jacket Community.” The article, while on the surface a discussion of fashion, could be read as mockery of the racial dimension of the Huang scandal.

After The New York Times’ Chinese-language edition introduced the commentary to its readers, a user on an anonymous Peking University forum accused the edition’s editors of displaying “the zeal of converts,” implying that their decision to publish criticism of a Chinese American business leader was an attempt to demonstrate loyalty to the West. The implication was that, by publishing a critical article in Chinese, the editors had somehow betrayed the Chinese community.

This tendency to interpret the scandal through ethnic identity thus also highlights some disturbing assumptions on the part of those who see Huang as a victim. Indeed, it seems at least some of those who highlight perceived racism against Huang have themselves absorbed antisemitic conspiracy theories originating in English-language social media. Some posts highlighted the Jewish backgrounds of executives at major American AI companies to insinuate that Jews secretly controlled the industry. Others invoked the Israeli backgrounds of potential Nvidia successors to allege a supposed Zionist takeover of AI.

Screenshots of these English-language posts were translated and circulated in Chinese-language WeChat groups I observed in Canada. While some Chinese-language commentators worried that Chinese women were being treated as potential spies and that Chinese American elites could never escape exclusion regardless of their achievements, antisemitic conspiracy theories from the English-speaking world were simultaneously entering Chinese-speaking communities, attributing developments in the United States’ AI industry to secret Jewish manipulation.

What is perhaps most striking is the divergence of narratives when talking about the same series of events. Some discuss a salacious scandal; some talk about U.S. export controls; some emphasize stereotypes about ethnic Chinese. Everyone sees a different Jensen Huang.
